claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten alloys under fusion-relevant conditions is governed predominantly by radiation-induced defect clusters.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten alloys under fusion-relevant conditions is governed predominantly by radiation-induced defect clusters.
Radiation-induced defect clusters act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Pinning by radiation-induced defect clusters increases yield stress.
Radiation-induced defect clusters alter strain-rate sensitivity.
Defect-cluster-mediated dislocation pinning delays plastic strain localization.
Delaying plastic strain localization enhances toughness.
In situ ion irradiation during high-temperature mechanical testing produces controlled defect clusters.
Approximately 1200–1400 °C represents a fusion-relevant high-temperature testing range for the proposed tungsten-alloy mechanism.
Radiation-generated defect clusters retard dislocation mobility.
Controlled dislocation pinning increases strain hardening.
Irradiated samples will have higher yield stress than matched non-irradiated controls.
Irradiated samples will exhibit greater strain hardening than matched non-irradiated controls.
Irradiated samples will exhibit more pinned dislocation structures than thermal-only and unperturbed controls.
The proposed mechanism may not hold when deformation is dominated solely by thermal effects.
The proposed mechanism may not hold where defect-annihilation kinetics differ substantially.
